To excrete means to push out or discharge waste substances from the body. When a living thing — a human, an animal, a plant, or even a tiny single cell — processes food, produces energy, or carries out any life function, it creates leftover materials that are useless or even poisonous to it. Excreting is the act of getting rid of those harmful or unnecessary leftovers.

Think of it like this: your body is a busy factory. Raw materials go in, useful things get made, but the process always leaves behind scraps and toxic byproducts. Excreting is how the factory throws out its trash.

The substances that get excreted are called waste products. These are not things the body chose to throw away carelessly — they are substances that must leave, because keeping them inside would cause damage or death. Common examples include:

  • Urine — Your kidneys filter your blood constantly and remove a waste chemical called urea (produced when your body breaks down protein), along with excess water and salts. This mixture is excreted as urine.
  • Carbon dioxide — Every cell in your body burns fuel for energy and produces CO₂ as a byproduct. Your lungs excrete this gas every single time you breathe out.
  • Sweat — Your skin excretes small amounts of waste salts and water through sweat glands, especially when you're hot or exercising.
  • Bile pigments — Your liver excretes certain waste chemicals into the digestive system, which eventually leave the body in feces.
An Important Distinction: Excretion vs. Secretion

These two words look and sound alike, but they mean very different things. This is one of the most common points of confusion, so pay close attention.

  • To excrete = to push waste out. The body no longer wants it. It's trash.
  • To secrete = to produce and release a useful substance. The body made it on purpose for a job.

For example, your pancreas secretes insulin — a hormone it deliberately produces to help control blood sugar. That is not excretion, because insulin is useful and intentional. But when your kidneys push urea-laced water out of your body as urine, that is excretion — because urea is a toxic waste that must be expelled.

A simple rule: if the body is releasing something useful, it's secretion. If it's releasing something unwanted or harmful, it's excretion.

In everyday life, people sometimes use "excrete" loosely to refer to any waste leaving the body, including feces. However, in precise biological language, feces are not a product of excretion — they are a product of egestion (also called defecation).

Here's why: feces are mostly made up of food that was never fully digested or absorbed — it passed through your digestive system without really becoming part of your body. Excretion, strictly speaking, deals with waste that was produced inside your body's cells as a result of chemical processes (metabolism). Urea, CO₂, and excess salts are true excretory products because they were generated within your body's working machinery.

That said, in casual conversation and even in some general-use writing, people do say things like "the body excretes waste" to include feces, and this is widely understood and accepted. Just know the precise biological meaning if accuracy matters.
Excretion Is Not Just a Human Thing

Every living organism excretes. This is one of the defining features of life itself.

  • Animals excrete through organs like kidneys, lungs, skin, and liver.
  • Plants excrete waste too — for example, they release oxygen (a byproduct of photosynthesis) through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata. Some plants also excrete excess salts through their leaves.
  • Single-celled organisms like bacteria excrete waste directly through their cell walls into their surroundings.

So "excrete" applies any time any living thing expels a metabolic waste product, regardless of how simple or complex that organism is.

Here is how the verb changes depending on how you use it:

  • Base form: excrete — "Kidneys excrete urea."
  • Third person singular (present): excretes — "The body excretes carbon dioxide through the lungs."
  • Past tense: excreted — "The fish excreted ammonia directly into the water."
  • Present participle: excreting — "The glands were excreting fluid at a high rate."

Here are sentences showing the word used correctly and naturally across different contexts:

  1. "Healthy kidneys excrete excess urea, salts, and water in the form of urine."
  2. "When you exercise, your skin excretes sweat to help cool your body down."
  3. "Every time you exhale, your lungs are excreting carbon dioxide produced by your cells."
  4. "The plant excretes oxygen as a byproduct of converting sunlight into food."
  5. "If the kidneys fail to excrete waste efficiently, toxic substances build up in the blood."
  6. "Scientists studied how marine animals excrete excess salt from the seawater they live in."

If you had to remember just one thing: to excrete is to expel metabolic waste from a living body — it is the biological act of throwing out the toxic or useless byproducts that the body's own chemical processes create, so that those substances don't accumulate and cause harm.
